Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]].

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be measurable spaces
([[def-measurable-space]]). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

Equivalently, the family

$$\mathcal{C}_f := \{\, B \subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \,\}$$

is a sigma-algebra on $Y$ containing $\mathcal{B}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

derivations.claim: For $1\le r\le m-1$ and $t\in\mathbb R$, $\{y_{(r)}\le t\}$ is the finite union over $r$-element index sets $J$ of $\bigcap_{j\in J}\{y_j\le t\}$, since at least $r$ remaining values are at most $t$ exactly when the $r$th ordered value is at most $t$. Each coordinate cylinder is measurable in the stated finite product structure by [F1] and [F3], so these sublevel sets are Borel. Since the closed left rays generate $\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$ by [F4], each order statistic is Borel by [F2]. The coordinate-deletion projection from $[0,1]^m$ to $[0,1]^{m-1}$ is measurable: preimages of measurable rectangles are finite intersections of coordinate cylinders, and the rectangles generate the product sigma-algebra by [F3]. Thus lifting a Borel set in the remaining-coordinate space gives a Borel set in the full product. If $y\le z$ coordinatewise, at least $r$ coordinates of $z$ are at most $z_{(r)}$; their corresponding coordinates of $y$ are also at most $z_{(r)}$, so $y_{(r)}\le z_{(r)}$. Every remaining-coordinate order statistic is therefore coordinatewise nondecreasing.

Fix $k$ and suppose $p_i\le c_k$. Rank $k$ passes exactly when at least $k-1$ other coordinates are at most $c_k$, which is $y_{(k-1)}\le c_k$; for $k=1$ this holds by $y_{(0)}=0$. For each $j>k$, since $p_i\le c_k\le c_j$, rank $j$ passes exactly when at least $j-1$ other coordinates are at most $c_j$, namely $y_{(j-1)}\le c_j$. Hence $R=k$ exactly when the first condition of $C_{i,k}$ holds and every higher rank fails, which is $p_{-i}\in C_{i,k}$. In that case $i$ must be among the first $k$ ranks: otherwise $p_{(k+1)}\le p_i\le c_k\le c_{k+1}$ would make rank $k+1$ pass. Conversely, if $R=k$ and $i$ is rejected, then $p_i\le p_{(k)}\le c_k$, rank $k$ passes and every higher rank fails, so the conditions defining $C_{i,k}$ hold.

For any remaining vector $y$, replace coordinate $i$ by $0$. Since $c_1>0$, rank one passes, so the resulting rejection count is some $r\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$. By step 2.1, $y\in C_{i,r}$; hence the sets cover the space. If $k<\ell$ and $y\in C_{i,k}$, its condition at $r=\ell-1$ gives $y_{(\ell-1)}>c_\ell$, while membership in $C_{i,\ell}$ would give $y_{(\ell-1)}\le c_\ell$. Thus the sets are disjoint. They are Borel by step 1.1 and their finite defining inequalities.

If $y\in C_{i,j}$ for some $j\le k<m$, the defining inequalities include $y_{(r)}>c_{r+1}$ for every $r\ge k$, so $D_{i,k}$ is contained in the displayed intersection. Conversely, suppose those inequalities hold and set $p_i=0$. Rank one passes, but no rank $\ell\ge k+1$ can pass: that would require $y_{(\ell-1)}\le c_\ell$, contrary to the assumed condition at $r=\ell-1$. Thus the rejection count is some $j\le k$, and step 2.1 puts $y$ in $C_{i,j}$. This proves the formula; when $k=m$, step 3.1 gives $D_{i,m}$ equal to the whole space. The formula is a finite intersection of Borel order-statistic superlevel sets and is coordinatewise increasing by step 1.1.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]), and fix an integer $m\ge1$ before observing the data. Write $[m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}$. A **finite family of null hypotheses** is a fixed list $H_{01},\ldots,H_{0m}$ with each $H_{0i}\subseteq\Theta$. For each $i\in[m]$, let $p_i:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$ be a p-value statistic ([[def-p-value]]). It is **valid for $H_{0i}$** when

$$P_\theta\{x:p_i(x)\le u\}\le u\qquad(\theta\in H_{0i},\ 0\le u\le1).$$

If $H_{0i}=\varnothing$, this universal condition is vacuous and $i$ never belongs to a true-null index set. For a nonempty null it agrees with the published valid-p-value definition. The family may have any joint dependence among its p-values. Validity is required only under the corresponding null laws; a p-value statistic alone does not imply validity.

For $\theta\in\Theta$, the **true-null index set** is
$$I_0(\theta):=\{i\in[m]:\theta\in H_{0i}\}.$$
A fixed deterministic multiple-testing rule is a family of measurable rejection events $D_i\in\mathcal A$, one for each $i\in[m]$. Its total number of rejections and number of false rejections at parameter $\theta$ are
$$R:=\sum_{i=1}^m\mathbf1_{D_i},\qquad V_\theta:=\sum_{i\in I_0(\theta)}\mathbf1_{D_i}.$$
Its **familywise error rate (FWER)** at $\theta$ is $P_\theta(V_\theta\ge1)$, and its **false discovery rate (FDR)** at $\theta$ is
$$E_\theta\!\left[\frac{V_\theta}{R\vee1}\right],$$
where $R\vee1=\max\{R,1\}$. The random variable $V_\theta/(R\vee1)$ is the **false discovery proportion (FDP)**. Strong FWER control at level $\alpha$ means that this FWER is at most $\alpha$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$, including parameters for which only some of the null hypotheses are true. The denominator convention makes the FDP zero when no hypothesis is rejected.

If the testing rule uses auxiliary randomization, include that randomizer in the observation and its sigma-algebra before defining the rejection events $D_i$.

These quantities are well-defined: the finite sums of indicators are measurable, $0\le V_\theta\le R$, and $0\le V_\theta/(R\vee1)\le1$, so the ratio is integrable under each probability law ([[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]).

Input an integer $m\ge1$, observed values $p_1,\ldots,p_m\in[0,1]$ of p-value statistics ([[def-p-value]]), and a target level $q\in(0,1)$. Let $H_m=\sum_{j=1}^m1/j$ be the harmonic number from [[def-harmonic-number-for-set-cover-analysis]]. For $k=1,\ldots,m$, set

$$c_k:=\frac{kq}{mH_m}.$$

Order the pairs $(p_i,i)$ lexicographically, so equal values are ordered by their original indices, and write the ordered values $p_{(1)}\le\cdots\le p_{(m)}$. Set

$$R:=\max\bigl(\{k\in\{1,\ldots,m\}:p_{(k)}\le c_k\}\cup\{0\}\bigr).$$

Reject exactly the hypotheses at ranks $1,\ldots,R$; when $R=0$, reject none. Because $H_m\ge1$, each critical value satisfies $0<c_k\le q/H_m\le q<1$. This definition specifies the procedure; no FDR guarantee is asserted here.

Let $m\ge1$, $p=(p_1,\ldots,p_m)\in[0,1]^m$, and critical values $0<c_1\le\cdots\le c_m\le1$. Give $[0,1]^m$ its finite product of the trace Borel sigma-algebras on $[0,1]$. Define the step-up rule by

$$R:=\max\bigl(\{k\in\{1,\ldots,m\}:p_{(k)}\le c_k\}\cup\{0\}\bigr),$$

rejecting exactly ranks $1,\ldots,R$. Fix $i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$. Give the remaining-coordinate space $[0,1]^{m-1}$ its finite product of the trace Borel sigma-algebras, with the empty product on the singleton empty tuple when $m=1$. Write the remaining values in increasing order as $y_{(1)}\le\cdots\le y_{(m-1)}$, and set $y_{(0)}=0$. For $1\le k\le m$, let

$$C_{i,k}:=\{y_{(k-1)}\le c_k\}\cap\bigcap_{r=k}^{m-1}\{y_{(r)}>c_{r+1}\},$$

with an empty intersection interpreted as the whole remaining-coordinate space. Put $D_{i,k}:=\bigcup_{j=1}^k C_{i,j}$. For $x\in[0,1]^m$, let $I_i(x)=1$ if the rule rejects coordinate $i$, and $I_i(x)=0$ otherwise. Then:

1. For every $k$, the following identity of subsets of $[0,1]^m$ holds:
   $$\{x\in[0,1]^m:I_i(x)=1,\ R(x)=k\}=\{x\in[0,1]^m:x_i\le c_k\}\cap\{x\in[0,1]^m:x_{-i}\in C_{i,k}\}.$$
   In particular, every input in the right-hand side has exactly $k$ rejections and rejects $i$.
2. The sets $C_{i,1},\ldots,C_{i,m}$ are a disjoint Borel partition of $[0,1]^{m-1}$.
3. For $k<m$,
   $$D_{i,k}=\bigcap_{r=k}^{m-1}\{y_{(r)}>c_{r+1}\},$$
   and $D_{i,m}$ is the whole space. Each $D_{i,k}$ is a coordinatewise increasing Borel set.

For $m=1$, the remaining-coordinate space is the singleton empty tuple with its full sigma-algebra, and $C_{i,1}=D_{i,1}$ is the whole space.

Let $p$ be a valid p-value for a nonempty null hypothesis $\Theta_0$ in a
statistical experiment. For every $\alpha\in[0,1]$, the deterministic test
with rejection function
$$\varphi_\alpha(x)=\mathbf 1_{\{p(x)\le\alpha\}}$$
satisfies
$$P_\theta(p(X)\le\alpha)=E_\theta[\varphi_\alpha(X)]\le\alpha \qquad(\theta\in\Theta_0).$$
Consequently, whenever a nonempty alternative hypothesis
$\Theta_1\subseteq\Theta\setminus\Theta_0$ is specified, this test has size
at most $\alpha$ and hence level $\alpha$ in the sense of
[[def-test-size-and-power]].

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space and let $A\in\mathcal F$.
Then the indicator $\mathbf 1_A$ satisfies
$$\mathbb E[\mathbf 1_A]=\mathbb P(A).$$

Let $X,Y$ be integrable real or complex random variables on one probability
space.

1. For scalars $a,b$,
   $$\mathbb E[aX+bY]=a\,\mathbb E[X]+b\,\mathbb E[Y].$$
2. If $X$ and $Y$ are real-valued and $X\le Y$ almost surely, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]\le\mathbb E[Y].$$
3. $$|\mathbb E[X]|\le\mathbb E[|X|].$$

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

derivations.claim: The bounded FDP is a finite sum over true-null indices and the realized rejection count; indicator expectation and finite linearity turn it into the displayed probability sum.
For each true-null coordinate, the step-up rejection partition and intervals J_j yield a weighted interval sum bounded by sum_j P(p_i∈J_j)/j.
The finite CDF differences telescope by summation by parts; superuniformity F_j≤jt gives the bound tH_m=q/m, including the zero endpoint.
Combining the per-null q/m bound with the finite true-null sum gives FDR≤(m_0/m)q≤q, with an empty outer sum when m_0=0.

boundaries.evidence: If there are no true nulls, the outer sum in step 1.1 is empty and step 3.1 gives FDR=0.
Validity at u=0 gives P(p_i=0)=0; step 1.2 removes that null event and step 2.1 sets F_0=0.
For m=1, H_1=1 and there is one interval; step 2.1 gives tH_1=q, equal to q/m.
The interval masses need not be bounded by their widths for discrete valid p-values; step 2.1 instead uses only F_j≤jt and finite summation by parts.
The level is q∈(0,1), mt=q/H_m<1, and validity is applied at all cutoffs jt including zero in steps 1.2–3.1.
Steps 1.1–4.1 use finite sums, a deterministic partition, and finite summation by parts; no choice principle or dependence assumption is used.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, let $m\ge1$, and let $\mathbf P=(P_1,\ldots,P_m):\Omega\to[0,1]^m$ be a random vector whose coordinates are p-value statistics ([[def-p-value]]). Fix a designated true-null index set $I_0\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}$. For $i\in I_0$, write $\mu_i$ for the law of $P_i$ under $\mathbb P$ and define its support relative to $[0,1]$ by

$$\operatorname{supp}(\mu_i):=\{x\in[0,1]:\mu_i(U)>0\text{ for every relatively open neighborhood }U\text{ of }x\}.$$

Give each coordinate $[0,1]$ its trace Borel sigma-algebra ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]) and give $[0,1]^m$ the finite product sigma-algebra ([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]). In this definition, “Borel set” means a member of that product sigma-algebra; thus “increasing measurable set” means coordinatewise increasing in this stated structure. The unit-interval lemma proves that $[0,1]$ with this trace Borel structure is standard Borel ([[lem-unit-interval-is-standard-borel]]). The finite-product result then makes $[0,1]^m$ with the specified product sigma-algebra a standard-Borel target ([[def-standard-borel-space]], [[lem-finite-products-of-standard-borel-spaces-are-standard-borel]]); its finite-product proof uses only finite choice in ZF. Under the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), this target has a regular conditional distribution given $\sigma(P_i)$, and the conditional-law factorization result supplies a kernel $K_i:[0,1]\to[0,1]^m$ representing the conditional law of $\mathbf P$ given $P_i=x$ ([[thm-existence-of-regular-conditional-distributions-for-standard-borel-targets]], [[lem-regular-conditional-kernels-factor-through-a-standard-borel-conditioning-variable]], [[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]]).

The law of $\mathbf P$ is **positive regression dependent on the true-null coordinates (PRDS on $I_0$)** if, for each $i\in I_0$, such a conditional-law version can be chosen so that for every coordinatewise increasing Borel set $D$, the function

$$x\longmapsto K_i(x,D)$$

is nondecreasing on $\operatorname{supp}(\mu_i)$. If $I_0=\varnothing$, this condition is vacuous. The monotonicity condition is a full conditional-law requirement; pairwise correlations alone do not verify it.

$$R:=\max\bigl(\{k\in\{1,\ldots,m\}:p_{(k)}\le c_k\}\cup\{0\}\bigr),$$

rejecting exactly ranks $1,\ldots,R$. Fix $i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$. Give the remaining-coordinate space $[0,1]^{m-1}$ its finite product of the trace Borel sigma-algebras, with the empty product on the singleton empty tuple when $m=1$. Write the remaining values in increasing order as $y_{(1)}\le\cdots\le y_{(m-1)}$, and set $y_{(0)}=0$. For $1\le k\le m$, let

$$C_{i,k}:=\{y_{(k-1)}\le c_k\}\cap\bigcap_{r=k}^{m-1}\{y_{(r)}>c_{r+1}\},$$

with an empty intersection interpreted as the whole remaining-coordinate space. Put $D_{i,k}:=\bigcup_{j=1}^k C_{i,j}$. For $x\in[0,1]^m$, let $I_i(x)=1$ if the rule rejects coordinate $i$, and $I_i(x)=0$ otherwise. Then:

1. For every $k$, the following identity of subsets of $[0,1]^m$ holds:
   $$\{x\in[0,1]^m:I_i(x)=1,\ R(x)=k\}=\{x\in[0,1]^m:x_i\le c_k\}\cap\{x\in[0,1]^m:x_{-i}\in C_{i,k}\}.$$
   In particular, every input in the right-hand side has exactly $k$ rejections and rejects $i$.
2. The sets $C_{i,1},\ldots,C_{i,m}$ are a disjoint Borel partition of $[0,1]^{m-1}$.
3. For $k<m$,
   $$D_{i,k}=\bigcap_{r=k}^{m-1}\{y_{(r)}>c_{r+1}\},$$
   and $D_{i,m}$ is the whole space. Each $D_{i,k}$ is a coordinatewise increasing Borel set.

For $m=1$, the remaining-coordinate space is the singleton empty tuple with its full sigma-algebra, and $C_{i,1}=D_{i,1}$ is the whole space.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ and $Y:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(T,\mathcal T)$ be measurable random elements. A **conditional law of X given Y** is a probability kernel $K:(T,\mathcal T)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ such that $\omega\mapsto K(Y(\omega),\cdot)$ is a regular conditional distribution of X given $\sigma(Y)$ in [[def-regular-conditional-distribution]]. Thus for every $A\in\mathcal S$ and $H\in\sigma(Y)$,
$$\int_H K(Y(\omega),A)\,dP=P(H\cap\{X\in A\}).$$

Composition with Y makes each evaluation $\sigma(Y)$-measurable, and every section remains a probability by [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. The notation $P(X\in A\mid Y=y)=K(y,A)$ refers to a chosen kernel; it is not a ratio involving the possibly zero probability $P(Y=y)$.

Write $P_Y(B)=P(Y^{-1}(B))$ for the law in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]. If a specified countable family $\mathcal C\subseteq\mathcal S$ determines probability measures, two conditional laws K,L agree as measures outside a single $\mathcal T$-measurable $P_Y$-null set. Indeed for each $A\in\mathcal C$ the measurable discrepancy $D_A=\{y:K(y,A)\ne L(y,A)\}$ has null inverse image under Y by [[lem-conditional-expectation-is-unique-almost-surely]]. Hence $P_Y(D_A)=0$ by the law definition; the countable union $D$ is null by [[thm-finite-and-countable-subadditivity-of-measures]], and off D the determining property gives equality of measures. This uses a supplied determining family and makes no AC assertion about obtaining one.

Values on a measurable $P_Y$-null subset may be replaced by a specified fixed probability on E without changing these identities. The inverse image of that subset is measurable null, and all event evaluations are bounded, so the modified event integrals agree. Empty-event evaluations remain zero and whole-target evaluations remain one. Existence on standard-Borel spaces is proved separately; the definition alone does not assert a conditional kernel exists.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space and let $A\in\mathcal F$.
Then the indicator $\mathbf 1_A$ satisfies
$$\mathbb E[\mathbf 1_A]=\mathbb P(A).$$

Let $X,Y$ be integrable real or complex random variables on one probability
space.

1. For scalars $a,b$,
   $$\mathbb E[aX+bY]=a\,\mathbb E[X]+b\,\mathbb E[Y].$$
2. If $X$ and $Y$ are real-valued and $X\le Y$ almost surely, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]\le\mathbb E[Y].$$
3. $$|\mathbb E[X]|\le\mathbb E[|X|].$$

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

Define $d_{\mathbb{R}} : \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ by
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) := |x - y|$ ([[def-abs-value]]). Then:

1. $d_{\mathbb{R}}$ is a metric on $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-metric-space]]); it is
   called the **usual metric** of $\mathbb{R}$.
2. For $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and $r > 0$ the open ball is the bounded open interval
   ([[def-interval]], [[def-metric-ball]])
   $$B(x,r) = (x-r,\ x+r),$$
   and the closed ball is $\bar B(x,r) = [x-r,\ x+r]$.
3. Consequently $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is open in the metric topology of
   $d_{\mathbb{R}}$ ([[def-metric-topology]]) exactly when for every $x \in U$
   there is $r > 0$ with $(x-r, x+r) \subseteq U$. This topology is called the
   **usual topology** of $\mathbb{R}$.
4. $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$ is not a bounded metric space
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]): no ball contains $\mathbb{R}$, so
   $\operatorname{diam}(\mathbb{R})$ is not defined.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]) and let
$S \subseteq X$. The **subspace topology** (also *relative topology*) on $S$ is

$$\mathcal{T}_S := \{\, U \cap S : U \in \mathcal{T} \,\},$$

the family of **traces** on $S$ of the open sets of $X$. The pair
$(S, \mathcal{T}_S)$ is a **subspace** of $X$. A subset of $S$ that lies in
$\mathcal{T}_S$ is said to be **open in $S$**, and *relatively open* where the
ambient space needs emphasis.

**$\mathcal{T}_S$ is a topology, and this is discharged here.** (T1):
$\varnothing = \varnothing \cap S$ and $S = X \cap S$ are traces. (T2): if
$\mathcal{S}' \subseteq \mathcal{T}_S$, choose for each member a set of
$\mathcal{T}$ tracing to it — no choice principle is needed, since
$U' := \bigcup \{\, U \in \mathcal{T} : U \cap S \subseteq W \,\}$ is a canonical
such set for $W \in \mathcal{T}_S$, being open by (T2) in $X$ and satisfying
$U' \cap S = W$ — and then
$\bigcup_i (U_i \cap S) = (\bigcup_i U_i) \cap S \in \mathcal{T}_S$ by (T2) in

**Closed sets of a subspace are the traces of the closed sets.** A set
$C \subseteq S$ is closed in $S$ if and only if $C = F \cap S$ for some closed
$F \subseteq X$. Indeed $S \setminus (U \cap S) = (X \setminus U) \cap S$ and
$S \setminus (F \cap S) = (X \setminus F) \cap S$, so complementation inside $S$
matches complementation inside $X$ under tracing.

$\mathcal{T}$ ([[def-topology-basis-subbasis]]) then
$\mathcal{B}_S := \{\, B \cap S : B \in \mathcal{B} \,\}$ is a basis for
$\mathcal{T}_S$: its members are open in $S$, and for $W = U \cap S$ open in $S$
and $x \in W$ there is $B \in \mathcal{B}$ with $x \in B \subseteq U$, whence
$x \in B \cap S \subseteq W$. The same computation with a subbasis $\mathcal{S}$
shows that $\{\, S_0 \cap S : S_0 \in \mathcal{S} \,\}$ is a subbasis for
$\mathcal{T}_S$, since tracing commutes with finite intersections and with
unions.

$\iota(s) = s$, satisfies $\iota^{-1}[U] = U \cap S$ for every $U \subseteq X$,

$\mathcal{T}_S$ is the **coarsest** topology on $S$ making $\iota$ continuous: any
topology on $S$ for which $\iota$ is continuous must contain every
$\iota^{-1}[U] = U \cap S$, hence contain $\mathcal{T}_S$.

**Characteristic property of a map into a subspace.** Let $(Z, \mathcal{T}_Z)$ be
a topological space and let $g : Z \to S$ be a function. Then

$$g \text{ is continuous as a map } Z \to (S,\mathcal{T}_S) \iff \iota \circ g \text{ is continuous as a map } Z \to (X,\mathcal{T}) .$$

*Proof.* For $U \in \mathcal{T}$ one has
$(\iota \circ g)^{-1}[U] = g^{-1}[\iota^{-1}[U]] = g^{-1}[U \cap S]$. If $g$ is
continuous then each $g^{-1}[U \cap S]$ is open, so $\iota \circ g$ is continuous;
conversely if $\iota \circ g$ is continuous then for any $W = U \cap S$ open in

$S \subseteq X$, then $f|_S : S \to Y$ is continuous, since
$(f|_S)^{-1}[V] = f^{-1}[V] \cap S$ is open in $S$ for every open $V \subseteq Y$
([[def-continuous-map-top]], [[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]]).

is open in $S$ if and only if it is open in $X$: a trace $U \cap S$ is then an
intersection of two open sets of $X$, and conversely an open subset of $X$

in $S$, and need be neither in $X$.

The map $q \mapsto \hat q$ ([[def-real-numbers]]) is an embedding of ordered
fields. Every real is approximated by rationals: for $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and
rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $q \in \mathbb{Q}$ with
$|x - \hat q| < \hat\varepsilon$. Consequently, strictly between any two
reals lies a rational.

$\mathbb{Q} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): the rationals are
countably infinite ([[def-countable]]).

and countability follows from a surjection without ever selecting a
representative. The same device handles $\mathbb{Z}$, which is a surjective image
of $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ by construction ([[def-integers]]).

**No choice principle is used**: the two enumerations are given, and the

Let $\mu$ be a measure and let $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be measurable. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k).$$

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ one also has

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k<m}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k<m}\mu(E_k),$$

including $m=0$, where both sides are $0$.

Let $A$ be a nonempty set. Then $A$ is at most countable ([[def-countable]]) if
and only if there is a surjection $s : \mathbb{N} \to A$
([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]).

Moreover, from any such surjection an injection $A \to \mathbb{N}$ is obtained
explicitly, without any choice, by

$$j(a) := \min\{\, k \in \mathbb{N} : s(k) = a \,\}.$$

This is the working form of countability used everywhere below: to prove a
nonempty set countable it suffices to list its elements, repetitions and all.

**No choice principle is used.** The backward direction is where an appeal to
choice would be natural ("for each $a$ pick some $k$ with $s(k) = a$") and it is
avoided outright, because $\min$ is canonical: every nonempty set of naturals has
a *least* element ([[thm-well-ordering-principle]]), so $j(a)$ is determined by
$a$ and $s$ alone.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if

measures on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ ([[def-measurable-space]],
[[def-probability-measure]]). The measures $P_\theta$ are the sampling laws.

the pushforward measure $P_X(B)=P(X^{-1}(B))$ from
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]; it is a probability measure by
[[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]].

The definition specifies the family of laws only. It supplies no sigma-algebra
on $\Theta$, no measurability condition on $\theta\mapsto P_\theta$, and no
common underlying probability space on which all observations must be realized.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]), and fix an integer $m\ge1$ before observing the data. Write $[m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}$. A **finite family of null hypotheses** is a fixed list $H_{01},\ldots,H_{0m}$ with each $H_{0i}\subseteq\Theta$. For each $i\in[m]$, let $p_i:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$ be a p-value statistic ([[def-p-value]]). It is **valid for $H_{0i}$** when

$$P_\theta\{x:p_i(x)\le u\}\le u\qquad(\theta\in H_{0i},\ 0\le u\le1).$$

If $H_{0i}=\varnothing$, this universal condition is vacuous and $i$ never belongs to a true-null index set. For a nonempty null it agrees with the published valid-p-value definition. The family may have any joint dependence among its p-values. Validity is required only under the corresponding null laws; a p-value statistic alone does not imply validity.

For $\theta\in\Theta$, the **true-null index set** is
$$I_0(\theta):=\{i\in[m]:\theta\in H_{0i}\}.$$
A fixed deterministic multiple-testing rule is a family of measurable rejection events $D_i\in\mathcal A$, one for each $i\in[m]$. Its total number of rejections and number of false rejections at parameter $\theta$ are
$$R:=\sum_{i=1}^m\mathbf1_{D_i},\qquad V_\theta:=\sum_{i\in I_0(\theta)}\mathbf1_{D_i}.$$
Its **familywise error rate (FWER)** at $\theta$ is $P_\theta(V_\theta\ge1)$, and its **false discovery rate (FDR)** at $\theta$ is
$$E_\theta\!\left[\frac{V_\theta}{R\vee1}\right],$$
where $R\vee1=\max\{R,1\}$. The random variable $V_\theta/(R\vee1)$ is the **false discovery proportion (FDP)**. Strong FWER control at level $\alpha$ means that this FWER is at most $\alpha$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$, including parameters for which only some of the null hypotheses are true. The denominator convention makes the FDP zero when no hypothesis is rejected.

If the testing rule uses auxiliary randomization, include that randomizer in the observation and its sigma-algebra before defining the rejection events $D_i$.

These quantities are well-defined: the finite sums of indicators are measurable, $0\le V_\theta\le R$, and $0\le V_\theta/(R\vee1)\le1$, so the ratio is integrable under each probability law ([[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]).

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Each coordinate has support $1/100,1/25,13/100,29/100,1$ and cumulative probabilities $1/100,4/100,13/100,29/100,1$, respectively. At each support value the cumulative probability equals that value; between successive support values it stays at the preceding value, and below $1/100$ it is zero. Thus $P(p_i\le u)\le u$ for every $u\in[0,1]$, so all four p-values are valid by [F2].
